This exercise takes about fifteen minutes and needs no materials. It works with two people or a whole group in pairs.

How to run it

  1. Form pairs. Decide who is A and who is B.
  2. A speaks for three minutes about a topic such as 'a time I changed my mind'. B only listens: no questions, no advice.
  3. B summarises what they heard in a minute, beginning with 'What I heard you say is...'.
  4. A says what was accurate and what was missed.
  5. Swap roles and repeat.

Debrief questions

  • What was hard about only listening?
  • What did it feel like to be listened to without interruption?
  • What did you notice about your own urge to respond?

Facilitator tip: keep the topic personal but low-risk. Never require anyone to share more than they wish.
resources.title: Three-Minute Listening Pairs
resources.description: A simple paired exercise for practising attentive listening.

resources.body:
Use this checklist before you answer in a conversation that matters.

  • Have I let the person finish?
  • Can I say in my own words what they mean?
  • Have I asked one question to check, rather than assumed?
  • Have I noticed how they feel, not only what they said?
  • Do I want to understand, or only to reply?
  • If I disagree, can I say what I do agree with first?

Practise with one conversation a day for a week and note what changes.
resources.title: Listening Before Responding: A One-Page Checklist
resources.description: A short checklist to use in everyday conversations.

resources.body:
Prepare

  1. What is the specific thing that happened? (facts only)
  2. How did it affect me?
  3. What do I want from this conversation?
  4. What might the other person's view be?
  5. What is my own part in the difficulty?
  6. When and where will we talk, and how will I give notice?

Opening line

Write one sentence that describes the event and its effect, using 'I' rather than 'you'. Example: 'When the plan changed without a message, I was left waiting and felt my time did not count.'

Afterwards, note what went well and what you would do differently.
resources.title: Difficult Conversation Planner
resources.description: A worksheet for preparing a conversation you have been avoiding.

resources.body:
Many disagreements stall because each side states a position (what they demand) rather than an interest (what they need).

Steps

  1. Each side writes their position in one sentence.
  2. Each side writes three reasons why it matters to them.
  3. Share the reasons only, without arguing.
  4. Together, list options that meet as many of the stated needs as possible.
  5. Choose one option to try and agree when to review it.

Use a low-stakes example first, such as how to share a room or a schedule.
resources.title: Interests, Not Positions: A Conflict Exercise
resources.description: A short exercise for finding what people need beneath what they demand.

resources.body:
For one week, write down each small commitment you make (for example, 'I will send that tomorrow'), and mark whether you kept it.

  • Day, commitment, to whom
  • Kept / not kept / renegotiated early
  • What I learned

At the end of the week, look for patterns. Do you over-promise? Do you tell people early when you cannot deliver? Trust grows when promises are modest and kept, or honestly renegotiated.
resources.title: The Promise Ledger
resources.description: A one-week practice to build reliability.

resources.body:
Week 1: Noticing

  • Describe a moment today when you felt a strong emotion. What happened just before?
  • What did you do with that feeling?

Week 2: Triggers

  • What kinds of remark make me defensive?
  • What am I protecting when I feel that way?

Week 3: Biases

  • Name an opinion you hold strongly. What would change your mind?
  • Whom have I judged quickly this week?

Week 4: Responsibility

  • What is mine to take responsibility for in a current difficulty?
  • What small step can I take this week?

Time: about 40 minutes. Materials: paper and pens.

  1. In small groups, students list what makes a discussion go well and what makes it go badly.
  2. Groups share and the class combines them into no more than five agreements.
  3. Rewrite each agreement as a positive action, such as 'We ask before we assume'.
  4. Everyone signs or agrees verbally. Display the agreements.
  5. Revisit them after two weeks and amend.

Teacher tip: model the agreements yourself, and refer to them gently when discussions heat up.

Before the first meeting

  • Decide who the circle is for and why.
  • Invite five to twelve people.
  • Find a quiet, accessible place or a reliable online platform.
  • Plan sixty to ninety minutes.

Structure of a session

  1. Welcome and agreements (10 minutes)
  2. Check-in: one sentence from each person (10 minutes)
  3. Theme and activity (30-40 minutes)
  4. Reflection and what we take away (15 minutes)
  5. Close (5 minutes)

Facilitation principles

  • Everyone may pass.
  • One voice at a time.
  • Speak from your own experience.
  • What is shared stays in the circle unless agreed.

List the decisions you make regularly. For each, mark one of the following:

  • I decide and inform others
  • I decide after asking for input
  • We decide together
  • I delegate the decision

Then ask: Which decisions could be shared more? Who would be affected? What support would others need? Choose one decision to change this month and note what happens.

resources.body: List five things you consider 'obvious' about daily life, such as how to greet a stranger or when a meeting should start. For each, write where you learned it and who might do it differently. Share with a partner and ask two open questions about their examples. Finish by writing one assumption you would like to hold more loosely.
resources.title: Assumption Audit
resources.description: An exercise for noticing the assumptions we treat as common sense.

circle_content.body: A Cooperation Circle is a small, regular gathering of five to twelve people who meet to talk, listen and practise cooperation together. A trained or experienced facilitator is helpful but not essential. Each circle chooses a theme, follows simple agreements and ends each session with something concrete to try before the next meeting. Circles can meet in a school, college, village hall, workplace or online.
circle_content.title: How Cooperation Circles work

circle_content.body: Start small and keep it simple. Agree on purpose, time and place. Invite people from different backgrounds where possible. Agree on confidentiality, one voice at a time, the right to pass and speaking from personal experience. Review after four sessions and adapt.
circle_content.title: Guidelines for starting a circle

circle_content.body: Teachers, students, community workers, volunteers, employees and neighbours can start a circle. You do not need to be an expert. If you want guidance, apply through the form and we will share the toolkit and available support.
circle_content.title: Who can start a circle

circle_content.body: Each person says one sentence about how they are arriving. No comments from others. This builds the habit of listening without responding.
circle_content.title: Activity: Check-in round

circle_content.body: In pairs, each person tells a short story about a custom, object or place that matters to them. The listener asks two open questions. Share one learning with the group.
circle_content.title: Activity: Story swap

circle_content.body: On a large sheet, the group writes what they share (concerns, hopes) in the middle and what differs at the edges. Discuss how differences might add to rather than subtract from shared goals.
circle_content.title: Activity: Common ground map

circle_content.body: Explore a time you changed your mind about a person or idea, and what made the change possible.
circle_content.title: Theme: When did I last change my mind?

circle_content.body: Discuss what fairness means in your own setting, such as a classroom or neighbourhood, and where it is hard.
circle_content.title: Theme: What does fairness look like here?

circle_content.body: Choose a shared local problem and explore small steps the circle could take.
circle_content.title: Theme: A problem we share

circle_content.body: Begin on time, restate the agreements, invite quieter voices by name without pressure, and gently return the group to the theme when it wanders. If emotions rise, slow down and name what you notice.
circle_content.title: Facilitation: Holding the space

circle_content.body: Treat disagreement as information. Ask each person to explain what matters to them about their view, and summarise before moving on. Remind the group that the aim is understanding, not agreement.
circle_content.title: Facilitation: When disagreement arises

circle_content.body: In groups of three, one speaks, one listens and one observes. The observer notes what helped the speaker feel heard. Rotate roles.
circle_content.title: Exercise: Listening in threes

circle_content.body: Choose a mild disagreement. Each person states the other's view so well that the other says 'Yes, that is it'. Only then do they give their own view.
circle_content.title: Exercise: The other side in my own words

stories.body: Illustrative example (not a report of a real event). Imagine a residents' group that gathers to clear a neglected lot. Older and younger neighbours who rarely spoke find themselves working side by side. Over tea afterwards, they begin to talk about what each wants from the space. Within a few weeks they have an informal rota for looking after it. The story shows how a modest shared task can create the conditions for cooperation.
stories.title: A Neighbourhood Clean-Up That Became a Conversation
stories.excerpt: Illustrative example: how a small shared task can open dialogue.

stories.body: Illustrative example (not a report of a real event). Imagine two schools in different neighbourhoods that agree to compile a shared local-history booklet. Students interview elders in each area and compare findings online. They discover how differently the same city looks from each side. The booklet is less important than the friendships that follow. The story illustrates inter-school collaboration.
stories.title: Two Schools, One Project
stories.excerpt: Illustrative example: peer learning between schools.

stories.body: Illustrative example (not a report of a real event). Imagine a village where households disagree over a shared water source. A small committee with members from each hamlet agrees to meet fortnightly, record decisions publicly and rotate the chair. Disagreements continue, but they are handled in the open, and the committee becomes a trusted forum. The story illustrates how fair process supports cooperation.

pages.body:
Why this initiative exists

Many of the problems people share, in families, schools, workplaces and across nations, are made harder by an inability to understand and work with those who differ from us. The Humanity & Cooperation Initiative exists to help people develop the understanding, skills and relationships needed to cooperate across differences, and to put that ability to work building a better shared future.

We believe cooperation begins with each of us: in the way we think, communicate, relate to others and take responsibility for our actions.

What cooperation across differences involves

Human connection. Cooperation starts with recognising one another as people.

Understanding. Seeing why others think and act as they do, without needing to agree.

Communication and listening. Speaking clearly, and listening to understand before replying.

Trust and empathy. Reliability over time, and the effort to imagine another's situation.

Responsibility and collaborative action. Owning our part, and working together on shared problems.

ORIVANA and The Humanity Movement

The Humanity & Cooperation Initiative is an ORIVANA initiative developed in collaboration with Randall S. Pitts and The Humanity Movement. ORIVANA is a global network for peace, education and humanity. Together, the partners aim to turn the ideas of cooperation into practical education, tools, conversations and community activity that anyone can use.

Randall S. Pitts and his mission

Randall S. Pitts collaborates with ORIVANA through The Humanity Movement. This section is awaiting the biography and mission statement approved by Randall S. Pitts. An administrator can add it from Admin → Pages → About.

Free for students and communities

Our articles, toolkit and learning resources are free to read and use. Students, teachers and community groups are never charged for core learning. The initiative is sustained through sponsorship, institutional programmes and voluntary contributions, described on the Support page.
